title: How to Handle Address Changes and Order Edits on Zendrop Before the Label Prints
excerpt: Address mistakes are cheap to fix before a label prints and expensive after. Here is the routing, validation, and reporting routine that keeps Zendrop order edits from turning into paid reshipments.
body: Customer address mistakes are one of the most expensive small problems in dropshipping. The order is already placed, the supplier has already started picking, and by the time the buyer notices the missing apartment number the parcel is heading to the wrong building. There is a short window between order placement and label creation where edits are still cheap, and the whole game is building a process that catches mistakes inside that window instead of after it.

Start by mapping the window itself. A Zendrop order moves from placement to processing to a shipping label, and each stage carries a different cost of change. Before the label exists, correcting a street line or a postal code is usually a data fix. After the label exists, the same correction becomes a carrier intercept request or a reshipment, and the margin on a single item order rarely survives that. Write down the timestamp boundaries you observe in your own account for your top two suppliers and treat those numbers as your internal service level.

The practical routing is simple. Support owns the first reply, operations owns the edit, and neither of them waits for the buyer to confirm twice. When a ticket contains an address correction, support replies within one business hour asking the buyer to restate the full shipping address in a single message, including apartment, company, and phone. Buyers who send a fragment create a second round trip, and a second round trip is usually the difference between catching the label and missing it.

Build a validation step into your own stack before the order ever reaches the supplier. Normalize the address fields at checkout, flag missing secondary lines, and hold orders with a mismatched city and postal code for a manual look. A five minute review of flagged orders each morning prevents most of the edits that would otherwise arrive as urgent tickets later in the day. This is the unglamorous half of the work, and it is where the money actually is.

When the label has already printed, stop thinking about edits and start thinking about outcomes. Contact the carrier with the tracking number for an intercept or a delivery address change, and decide in advance who pays for the second shipment. A clear policy helps here: if the buyer submitted a wrong address, offer a paid reshipment at cost; if your own validation let a bad address through, absorb it and log the cause. Either way, tell the buyer what happens next with a date rather than a vague promise.

Track the outcome in one small report: edits caught before the label, edits caught after the label, and reshipment cost per month. The first number should rise and the second should fall as your checkout validation improves. Zendrop order data makes this easy to pull, and the pattern tells you whether the real problem is buyer error or a form on your own site.
